paragraphs: The paper studies how to identify the best K items when the available evidence consists of noisy comparisons between pairs. It distinguishes two goals: finding those items in the correct order, and simply finding the set of best items. Keeping these goals separate matters because identifying membership and resolving order place different demands on the comparisons collected.

The approach is active: the procedure can choose which comparisons to collect, potentially making those choices sequentially. The authors analyze both goals under a noise model broad enough to include several established comparison models. They give upper bounds on the number of comparisons required and present an algorithm that applies to both sorting and partitioning.

The analysis shows that active selection can substantially reduce the comparison budget relative to passive ranking. The size of this multiplicative advantage depends on the underlying noise model. Thus, the contribution identifies circumstances in which choosing comparisons strategically offers a provable efficiency benefit, rather than promising one fixed improvement across every ranking problem.
icml-2017-active-learning-for-top-k-rank.tldr: Choosing noisy pairwise comparisons actively can substantially reduce the samples needed to identify or order the top K items.

paragraphs: Optimization methods often choose a training example or a block of features at random before taking an update. Uniform sampling treats these choices equally, even when some produce larger gradients than others. This paper investigates how to exploit that uneven structure without spending so much effort choosing updates that the benefit disappears.

The authors use a bandit optimization procedure to learn sampling probabilities during optimization. Depending on the underlying method, these probabilities determine which coordinates or examples receive attention. The framework applies to nonsmooth problems and is designed to discover useful sampling structure at low computational cost. Its guarantee compares performance with the best stationary sampling distribution, meaning a distribution that remains fixed.

When the relevant structure exists, the resulting convergence guarantees are tighter than those for nonadaptive methods. That condition is central: the improvement comes from learning differences among available updates. Experiments on several datasets complement the theoretical analysis, supporting the idea that sampling itself can be learned as part of the optimization process.
icml-2017-adaptive-sampling-probabilitie.tldr: A low-cost bandit procedure learns which examples or coordinates to sample, improving convergence guarantees when useful gradient structure exists.

paragraphs: Matrix completion fills in missing entries by exploiting structure in the data. This paper extends the usual low-rank view to data lying on an algebraic variety: a set described by polynomial equations. Such data can form a high-rank matrix in its original representation while still having exploitable nonlinear structure.

The key step maps each data column into a larger collection of monomial features, where the resulting matrix becomes low-rank. This framework covers affine subspaces and unions of them, as well as higher-degree curves and surfaces. The proposed algorithm minimizes a convex or nonconvex approximation to the lifted matrix's rank. A kernel computation avoids explicitly constructing that potentially large feature representation.

The authors study how many observations recovery requires, with particular attention to unions of affine subspaces. Synthetic experiments recover data up to the predicted sampling bounds, while real-data experiments outperform standard techniques. These results support nonlinear structure as a useful basis for completion even when low rank is absent from the original matrix.
icml-2017-algebraic-variety-models-for-h.tldr: Polynomial structure enables matrix completion by making potentially high-rank data low-rank in an implicit expanded feature space.

paragraphs: Hidden units can help time-series models represent long-term dependencies and complex relationships, but they also make parameter learning difficult. This paper asks whether the direction in which a sequence is modeled can help address that difficulty. Its proposal trains both an ordinary forward model and a model of the time-reversed sequence.

The two models share parameters. The central observation is that the parameters that are difficult to learn in one direction form a complementary subset to those that are difficult in the other. Training both directions therefore provides a way to improve estimates of parameters that would be poorly learned from either direction alone.

The authors apply this bidirectional learning procedure to a dynamic Boltzmann machine extended with hidden units. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate advantages for the approach. The contribution is a training strategy that uses complementary information from temporal directions: reversing the sequence becomes a means of learning shared parameters more effectively, rather than merely another way to present the data.
icml-2017-bidirectional-learning-for-tim.tldr: Training shared-parameter time-series models in both temporal directions helps learn parameters that are difficult to estimate in either direction alone.

paragraphs: Clustering becomes difficult when each observation combines continuous measurements with discrete attributes. The paper addresses this setting through a probabilistic model of how such mixed data is generated. Its tree-structured graphical model expresses the joint distribution as a product of pairwise interactions, localizing relationships between variables of different types.

The method then treats the estimated density as a landscape. Density peaks serve as centers, and their attractive basins organize observations into clusters. This connects the probabilistic description of the data to a geometric account of grouping: clusters correspond to regions associated with peaks in the modeled distribution.

Small peaks can create divisions that do not yield meaningful clusters. To address this, the approach uses ideas from topological data analysis to adaptively merge trivial peaks into larger ones. The authors report that the resulting method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on mixed-type data. Its contribution combines a model for heterogeneous attributes with a way to simplify the density landscape when forming clusters.
icml-2017-composing-tree-graphical-model.tldr: A tree-based probabilistic model and topology-guided peak merging produce clusters for data containing both continuous and discrete attributes.

paragraphs: The paper develops methods for training generative adversarial networks to synthesize images conditioned on class labels. Its GAN variant generates images at 128 by 128 resolution that exhibit coherence across the image as a whole. Label conditioning makes the intended class part of the generation problem.

The authors also introduce two analyses for assessing generated images: how clearly samples communicate their class and how much diversity they display within classes. These questions distinguish recognizable category information from variation among generated examples. The resolution analysis shows that higher-resolution samples contain class information that is absent from lower-resolution samples.

Across 1,000 ImageNet classes, the 128 by 128 samples are more than twice as discriminable as artificially resized 32 by 32 samples. Separately, samples for 84.7% of classes show diversity comparable to real ImageNet data. These findings support both the value of the higher-resolution output and the importance of examining diversity alongside class recognizability, while keeping the two reported properties distinct.
icml-2017-conditional-image-synthesis-wi.tldr: A label-conditioned GAN produces coherent 128 by 128 images, with analyses showing stronger class information and substantial within-class diversity.

paragraphs: Count-based exploration encourages a reinforcement learning agent to investigate unfamiliar situations. Earlier work extended this idea beyond explicit state tables by deriving a pseudo-count from a density model and using it to provide an exploration bonus. This paper examines two ingredients of that approach: the density model and a mixed Monte Carlo update.

The authors use PixelCNN, a neural image density model, to generate pseudo-counts. Doing so requires addressing difficulties that arise when assumptions of the earlier method are violated. Their adaptation produces a more practical and general algorithm, and they combine the resulting pseudo-counts with different agent architectures.

The reported experiments substantially improve the state of the art on several difficult Atari games. They also reveal that the mixed Monte Carlo update strongly facilitates exploration when rewards are especially sparse, including in Montezuma's Revenge. The findings therefore connect exploration performance to both novelty estimation and the agent's update procedure, rather than attributing the reported gains solely to a more advanced density model.
icml-2017-count-based-exploration-with-n.tldr: PixelCNN-based pseudo-counts improve exploration on difficult Atari games, while mixed Monte Carlo updates prove especially helpful with sparse rewards.

paragraphs: Answering a natural-language question about a table can require several connected execution steps. The paper considers two ways to perform them. A distributed neural executor supports end-to-end training but has weaknesses in execution efficiency and explicit interpretability. A symbolic executor runs efficiently but is difficult to train, especially at the beginning.

The proposed approach couples these executors during learning. Intermediate results from the distributed executor are used to pretrain the symbolic executor one step at a time. This gives the symbolic component guidance about the sequence of operations, using information already produced inside the trainable neural execution process.

Experiments show that the combined approach significantly outperforms both distributed and symbolic executors, with high accuracy, learning efficiency, execution efficiency, and interpretability. The result illustrates the value of transferring intermediate execution knowledge between representations. The distributed executor helps establish how a query should be carried out, while the symbolic executor brings the efficient and explicit execution properties that motivated its use.
icml-2017-coupling-distributed-and-symbo.tldr: Step-by-step guidance from a distributed executor helps train a symbolic table-query executor, improving accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability in experiments.

paragraphs: When several agents learn together, each may observe only part of the environment and have limited communication with teammates. Because those teammates are also exploring, an agent's local experience can appear to come from a changing environment. This paper formalizes the additional challenge of learning across multiple tasks under these conditions.

Maintaining a separate policy for every task creates two problems: agents must learn and store multiple policies, and choosing among them requires knowing which task is active. The paper specifically addresses settings where task identity is not directly observable. It first introduces a decentralized approach for learning a single task that is robust to teammates' concurrent interactions.

The next step distills the single-task policies into one policy that performs well across related tasks without receiving an explicit task identity. This links learning under interacting teammates with learning behavior shared across tasks. The resulting formulation makes hidden task identity part of the problem itself, rather than assuming an external label will select the appropriate specialized policy.
icml-2017-deep-decentralized-multi-task-.tldr: Decentralized learning and policy distillation produce a unified multi-agent policy for related tasks without explicit task identities.

paragraphs: Sensor-driven neural networks often have activations that change little between nearby moments. Delta networks exploit this temporal stability in recurrent neural networks: a neuron transmits its value only when its activation changes by more than a threshold. The goal is to reduce repeated computation and memory access when little has changed.

This is particularly relevant to recurrent networks because their states must be stored and fetched at every timestep. A straightforward runtime implementation provides only modest savings. The paper therefore develops optimized training techniques that achieve greater acceleration while maintaining higher accuracy, making training part of the efficiency strategy.

With these optimizations, the authors report a ninefold cost reduction on TIDIGITS with negligible accuracy loss. Trained delta networks show a 5.7-fold improvement on Wall Street Journal speech recognition, also with negligible accuracy loss, and pretrained networks can be accelerated as well. In a driving model combining convolutional and recurrent components, the recurrent component's cost falls by 100 times. That final figure concerns the RNN portion of the network.
icml-2017-delta-networks-for-optimized-r.tldr: Delta networks transmit recurrent activations only after sufficiently large changes, substantially reducing computation in the reported sensor tasks.

paragraphs: Many data summarization problems can be expressed as selecting a useful subset through submodular maximization. Efficient approximation algorithms already address this broad framework, but their usefulness does not automatically protect people whose sensitive data contributes to the summary. This paper makes differential privacy an explicit part of the optimization problem.

The authors develop privacy-preserving algorithms for both monotone and nonmonotone objectives, covering cases where adding elements does or does not always improve the objective. They address cardinality, matroid, and p-extendible system constraints, which specify different restrictions on the subsets that may be selected. The resulting guarantees are described as competitive with optimal guarantees.

The study also produces a contribution beyond privacy: a new nonmonotone maximization algorithm with a constant approximation ratio and linear running time. The authors identify it as the first to combine those properties even without a privacy requirement. Two experiments validate the algorithms' efficacy. Together, the contributions connect privacy-aware summarization with advances in the underlying optimization machinery.
icml-2017-differentially-private-submodu.tldr: The paper develops differentially private submodular maximization algorithms and a linear-time constant-approximation algorithm for nonmonotone maximization.

paragraphs: McGan approaches generative adversarial network training through a statistical comparison between distributions. The paper introduces families of integral probability metrics, which provide a loss for comparing the distribution of generated examples with the distribution being modeled. The comparison takes place after distributions are represented in a finite-dimensional feature space.

The proposed metrics focus on feature means and covariances. Means describe average feature values, while covariances describe how features vary together. Matching these statistics gives the training objective a concrete interpretation: generated and target distributions are compared through selected properties of their feature representations. Both average behavior and relationships among features therefore enter the formulation.

The authors state that these mean- and covariance-matching metrics allow stable GAN training and give McGan a meaningful loss between distributions. The contribution centers on how the training objective is defined. By expressing the discrepancy through feature statistics, the method connects the quantity being minimized to identifiable statistical differences between generated data and the data the model seeks to reproduce.
icml-2017-mcgan-mean-and-covariance-feat.tldr: McGan trains GANs using distribution metrics that match feature means and covariances, supporting stable training with a meaningful loss.

paragraphs: Neural networks can perform well with abundant labeled data, yet rapidly learning a new concept from few examples remains difficult. The challenge also includes preserving performance on concepts learned earlier. Meta Networks, or MetaNet, addresses this broader problem by learning knowledge across tasks that can support adaptation to new ones.

The method uses fast parameterization to shift its inductive biases: the preferences that guide how it generalizes from limited observations. Knowledge accumulated at a meta level therefore influences how the model responds to a particular task. The central idea is to learn an adaptation mechanism across tasks so that a small amount of new training data can become more useful.

On Omniglot and Mini-ImageNet, the authors describe performance as near human level and report improvements over baseline approaches of up to 6% accuracy. They also demonstrate properties relevant to generalization and continual learning. These are benchmark findings supporting rapid adaptation; the abstract presents maintaining earlier knowledge as part of the motivating challenge and reports related continual-learning properties.
icml-2017-meta-networks-323f5a0002.tldr: MetaNet learns across tasks to rapidly adjust its parameters and generalize from few examples, with strong results on two benchmarks.

paragraphs: Attention-based recurrent encoder-decoder models allow speech recognition components to be trained together by handling alignment between audio and the output sequence. This paper extends that end-to-end approach to recordings from multiple microphones. It brings microphone-array processing for noise suppression and speech enhancement inside the acoustic encoding network.

The resulting architecture jointly optimizes beamforming components with the recognition system. Beamforming combines information from the microphone channels, so its role is directly connected to how the recognizer processes noisy speech. Joint optimization allows this signal-processing component to be shaped by the final speech recognition objective.

Experiments use the noisy speech benchmarks CHiME-4 and AMI. The multichannel system outperforms an attention-based baseline that receives input from a conventional adaptive beamformer. This comparison supports integrating microphone processing into the learned recognition architecture. The contribution expands what can be optimized end to end, linking the treatment of multiple audio channels to the same objective used to learn the rest of the recognizer.
icml-2017-multichannel-end-to-end-speech.tldr: Jointly training microphone-array processing with speech recognition improves results over a conventional beamforming baseline on two noisy speech benchmarks.

paragraphs: The Nyström method constructs a low-rank approximation of a kernel matrix using selected landmarks. Which landmarks are chosen affects the quality of that approximation. Earlier empirical work suggested that landmarks derived from kernel clustering work well, but the approach lacked a theoretical guarantee on its approximation error.

This paper supplies the first such bound for landmarks selected through kernel K-means++ sampling. The result gives a mathematical basis for a choice that had previously been supported empirically. It connects a specific landmark-selection procedure to control of the error in the resulting matrix approximation.

For the Gaussian kernel, the authors also provide theoretical motivation for refining the selected landmarks through Lloyd updates in the original instance space. This addresses both initial landmark selection and subsequent refinement. Comparisons with several state-of-the-art algorithms substantiate the theoretical results empirically. The contribution is therefore an explanation of why these clustering-based landmarks can be effective, together with evidence about their use in practical approximation procedures.
icml-2017-nystrom-method-with-kernel-k-m.tldr: The paper establishes an approximation-error bound for Nyström landmarks chosen by kernel K-means++ and motivates refinements for Gaussian kernels.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference is meant to incorporate prior knowledge, but computational convenience often influences which prior is used. This paper asks whether inference can first use a convenient substitute prior and then be transformed to reflect a desired prior. The aim is to reuse completed inference while changing the prior information it incorporates.

Importance sampling is a possible route, but the authors show that it fails for many target priors, depending on their form and similarity to the substitute prior. They instead propose prior swapping, which uses the already inferred substitute posterior to efficiently generate accurate samples from the posterior associated with an arbitrary target prior.

The method allows less costly inference algorithms to be used for certain models and makes it possible to incorporate new or revised prior information after inference. The authors provide theoretical guarantees and demonstrations across multiple models and priors. The contribution separates the computational role of a convenient initial prior from the substantive prior knowledge that should ultimately shape the posterior.
icml-2017-post-inference-prior-swapping-.tldr: Prior swapping reuses inference under a convenient substitute prior to generate posterior samples incorporating a desired or updated prior.

paragraphs: A feature can have its own description in addition to the values it takes across training examples. The paper calls these vector descriptions feature side-information. Such descriptions may capture intrinsic properties of features, yet standard learning often ignores them or uses them only to choose features before fitting a model.

The proposed framework incorporates this information during learning across very general model families. It controls the structure of the learned model so that the model reflects similarities among features, with those similarities defined using the side-information. Descriptions of the inputs therefore influence how the predictive model is organized.

Experiments on several benchmark datasets show significant predictive gains over multiple baselines when the side-information is used. The findings support treating information about features as a resource for model fitting itself. The contribution is especially relevant to nonlinear modeling because it offers a framework for connecting feature relationships to learned structure, rather than leaving those descriptions outside the prediction-learning process.
icml-2017-regularising-non-linear-models.tldr: Using descriptions of features to guide model structure improves prediction across the reported benchmark experiments.

paragraphs: SARAH addresses finite-sum minimization, where an objective combines many component terms. The paper introduces both the main algorithm and a practical variant, SARAH+. Its defining feature is a simple recursive procedure for updating stochastic gradient estimates, providing a different update framework from ordinary stochastic gradient descent and several established stochastic methods.

The recursion also has a storage benefit relative to SAG and SAGA: SARAH does not need to retain past gradients. This matters because the gradient estimate can be updated without maintaining that historical collection. The contribution concerns how useful gradient information is carried forward through optimization steps.

Under strong convexity, the authors prove a linear convergence rate for SARAH. They also establish linear convergence for its inner loop in that same setting, a property they state SVRG does not possess. Numerical experiments demonstrate the algorithm's efficiency. The strong-convexity assumption is essential to the stated rates, while the experiments provide a separate empirical assessment of the recursive method's practical performance.
icml-2017-sarah-a-novel-method-for-machi.tldr: SARAH recursively updates stochastic gradient estimates without storing past gradients and has linear convergence guarantees under strong convexity.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to revise a sequence to improve an associated outcome after learning only from sequence–outcome pairs. It does not require examples showing how to improve a sequence, or additional evaluations of proposed revisions. This makes the learned relationship between sequences and outcomes central to the revision process.

A recurrent variational autoencoder represents sequences through continuous latent factors, while a neural prediction module estimates their outcomes. The components are learned through joint approximate inference. Revision then uses gradients to optimize the continuous representation with respect to predicted outcomes, avoiding a combinatorial search directly over sequence elements.

The optimization is constrained, and the decoder converts the adjusted representation back into a sequence. The intended result preserves fundamental similarity to the original, looks natural, and has a better associated outcome. The paper proves these properties with high probability under its approach and demonstrates the method on natural-language sentences. The guarantees belong to the proposed model and constrained procedure, preserving the distinction between inferred outcomes and newly measured evaluations.
icml-2017-sequence-to-better-sequence-co.tldr: A sequence model revises inputs by optimizing continuous latent factors for predicted outcomes while constraining similarity and naturalness.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks must retain information from earlier inputs to learn dependencies over time. LSTMs and GRUs address this with sophisticated gated architectures. This paper introduces the statistical recurrent unit, or SRU, which learns long-term dependencies using moving averages of statistics without a gating mechanism.

The design makes running statistical summaries the basis of its memory. Although the architecture is simpler and ungated, its parameter count is comparable to that of LSTMs. The comparison therefore explores whether a different way of maintaining information can be competitive with more elaborate recurrent units, without claiming that simplicity necessarily means fewer parameters.

The authors evaluate synthetic and real-world tasks, optimizing the hyperparameters of each architecture to make the comparison fair. SRUs perform favorably against LSTMs and GRUs and often outperform one or both. These findings show that moving statistical summaries can support effective recurrent learning across the tested tasks. They provide empirical support for the architecture without asserting that it wins every comparison.
icml-2017-the-statistical-recurrent-unit.tldr: The ungated statistical recurrent unit learns long-term dependencies through moving averages and performs competitively with LSTMs and GRUs.

paragraphs: The paper investigates what a feed-forward neural network does to its inputs, using speech recognition as a case study. Its empirical framework examines the information encoded in node activations across layers. It also reconstructs the exact function applied to an individual data point in the form of a linear transform.

These two views connect internal representations with the computation that produces the network's response. The authors apply them to networks trained to map acoustic features to phoneme labels. Considering the transform for each data point provides a way to investigate how the overall nonlinear model acts on different inputs.

The study finds selective, nonlinear warping of the feature space, achieved through prototypical functions that account for variation within each class. This describes how different input variations are handled as the network forms its classification. The contribution is a joint analytical framework: activation patterns and input transformations can be studied together, allowing the properties of learned representations to be linked to the functions the network implements.
icml-2017-understanding-the-representati.tldr: An empirical framework links network activations to input-specific transforms, revealing selective nonlinear feature-space warping in speech recognition networks.

paragraphs: Adaptive gradient methods adjust their updates during optimization and are widely useful in training neural networks. This paper studies their theoretical behavior in online convex optimization. In that setting, regret measures accumulated performance relative to a comparison choice, so a bound describes how that accumulated gap grows as learning proceeds.

The authors establish a square-root-in-T type regret bound for RMSProp. They then introduce SC-Adagrad and SC-RMSProp, two variants with logarithmic regret bounds for strongly convex functions. Logarithmic growth provides a stronger dependence on the number of rounds, but the stated result specifically relies on strong convexity.

Experiments evaluate both strongly convex optimization and deep neural network training. The new variants outperform other adaptive gradient methods or stochastic gradient descent in the reported experiments. The paper therefore combines theoretical guarantees in a structured optimization setting with empirical evidence in neural network training. The strong-convexity condition governs the logarithmic guarantees; the neural network findings are presented as experimental results.
icml-2017-variants-of-rmsprop-and-adagra.tldr: SC-Adagrad and SC-RMSProp achieve logarithmic regret under strong convexity and show favorable optimization and neural network training results.

paragraphs: Variational dropout gives Gaussian dropout a Bayesian interpretation. This paper extends that approach to allow unbounded dropout rates and investigates assigning an individual dropout rate to each network weight. It also proposes a way to reduce the variance of the gradient estimator used during learning.

The reported outcome is extreme sparsity in both fully connected and convolutional layers: the learned solution uses far fewer parameters. The authors relate this behavior to automatic relevance determination in empirical Bayes. The individual treatment of weights connects the learning procedure to determining which parts of a network remain useful.

Experiments reduce parameter counts by up to 280 times on LeNet architectures and up to 68 times on VGG-like networks, with negligible decreases in accuracy. These are the largest reported reductions for those architecture families, rather than a uniform compression factor for every network. The findings show that this extension of variational dropout can serve as a powerful sparsification mechanism while preserving nearly all measured accuracy in the reported cases.
icml-2017-variational-dropout-sparsifies.tldr: Variational dropout with individual per-weight rates produces highly sparse networks, with large reported parameter reductions and negligible accuracy loss.

paragraphs: The paper investigates why posterior sampling for reinforcement learning performs much better in computational results than existing optimism-driven algorithms such as UCRL2. Its goal is both to assess the size of this advantage and to understand the phenomenon responsible for it. This connects observed algorithm behavior with a theoretical account of learning performance.

Using that insight, the authors prove a Bayesian regret bound of order H√(SAT), up to logarithmic factors, for finite-horizon episodic Markov decision processes. The previous best bound described in the abstract has order HS√(AT), also up to logarithmic factors. The improvement changes the dependence on S from linear to square-root while retaining the other displayed factors.

Extensive empirical evaluation supports the theoretical results. The contribution combines an improved Bayesian regret guarantee with evidence about the performance gap motivating the study. Its theoretical setting is specifically finite-horizon episodic decision processes, and the strong empirical comparison concerns the evaluated algorithms. Together, these results provide support for posterior sampling from both analysis and computation.
icml-2017-why-is-posterior-sampling-bett.tldr: The paper explains posterior sampling's empirical advantage and proves an improved Bayesian regret bound for finite-horizon episodic reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a reinforcement learning problem in which an agent first acquires skills for subtasks and then uses them to execute instruction sequences. It distinguishes generalizing to previously unseen instructions from generalizing to longer instruction sequences. These require both recognizing relationships among tasks and organizing skills across time.

For unseen instructions, the authors propose an objective that encourages analogies between similar subtasks. For sequences, they introduce a hierarchical architecture whose meta controller learns to use acquired skills to follow instructions. A further neural component learns when to update the active subtask, improving learning efficiency in the presence of delayed rewards.

Experiments in a stochastic three-dimensional domain show that these proposed ideas are crucial to generalization to both unseen and longer instructions. The contribution brings together learning correspondences, composing skills, and deciding when to move between subtasks. It is presented as a step toward zero-shot task generalization, with the reported evidence tied to the instruction-following problem and domain studied.
icml-2017-zero-shot-task-generalization-.tldr: Analogy-based learning and hierarchical skill control help a reinforcement learning agent generalize to unseen instructions and longer instruction sequences.
